title: Revenue Booked Before the Truck Left
scenario: Anneliese Fischbach is the audit senior on a mid-sized machinery maker in Bavaria. At year end, the finance director records a large order as revenue, although the goods ship in early January. He says the customer has accepted the terms and the delay is purely logistical. The booking lets the company meet a covenant on its bank loan. Anneliese's partner is reluctant to challenge a client of twenty years. If the covenant is breached, the bank could call the loan and put six hundred jobs at risk.
options: Insist the revenue be reversed into the next year and, if refused, qualify the audit opinion.
Accept the booking if the customer provides written confirmation of transfer of control before year end, and document the judgement.
Defer to her partner's decision on the client relationship and record her disagreement internally.

title: A Pension Trustee Asked to Chase Returns
scenario: Sibusiso Ncube chairs the trustees of a mining workers' pension fund in Bulawayo. A fund manager proposes shifting a quarter of assets into a property development owned by a politically connected businessman, promising double the return of government bonds. The fund is underfunded and retirees' payments have been cut once. The development is unfinished, and the appraisals come from the sponsor. Several trustees feel pressure from the union leadership, which wants higher returns now. Others fear the loss of retirees' last security.
options: Reject the investment and focus on lower-risk assets, accepting that benefits may stay reduced.
Approve a much smaller allocation conditional on independent valuation and staged release of funds.
Approve the full allocation, given the underfunding and the pressure to restore benefits.
tension: retirees' security vs. need for returns

title: The Inventory That Existed Only on Paper
scenario: Rina Halim is an internal auditor at an Indonesian electronics distributor in Surabaya. During a stock count she finds that about a tenth of the warehouse inventory listed as 'in stock' does not physically exist. The warehouse manager says the items were damaged and he did not want to report losses before bonus season. Writing off the stock would reduce profits, and with them bonuses across the company. The warehouse manager is close to the owner. The owner is about to apply for a bank loan based on this year's figures.
options: Report the discrepancy in full to the audit committee and recommend an immediate write-off before any loan application.
Give the warehouse manager a short chance to document the damage properly, then report the corrected figures.
Raise the matter verbally with the owner only, allowing him to decide how to restate the figures.

title: A Trustee's Mother Wants Her Savings Back
scenario: Colm Gallagher, a trustee and accountant for a small credit union in Galway, learns that the manager has made several loans to a local developer that are now unlikely to be repaid, but has classified them as performing. If the loans are reclassified, the union may breach capital requirements and face merger with a larger bank. Colm's own mother holds her life savings there. Telling the regulator promptly is required by his duties, yet a quiet rescue by members may avoid panic. A members' meeting is scheduled for next week.
options: Notify the regulator now about the misclassified loans, accepting the consequences for the union.
Inform the board and demand reclassification and a recovery plan before involving the regulator.
Say nothing before the members' meeting, hoping the developer can repay and no member suffers.

title: The Tax Shelter That Looks Too Clever
scenario: Hiroshi Nakagawa, a tax advisor at a Tokyo firm, designs structures for wealthy clients. A client's request is for a layered arrangement of foreign holding entities that would legally reduce tax to nearly zero, though its only purpose is to avoid tax and its commercial substance is thin. The law as written appears to allow it, but regulators have criticised similar schemes. The client is a major source of fees. Hiroshi's partner says every aggressive structure carries some risk, and clients ultimately decide.
options: Decline to design the structure, explaining that its lack of substance goes against his professional standards.
Design it with a written explanation of the regulatory risk and require the client's explicit acknowledgement.
Design it as requested, since it is lawful as the rules currently stand and clients are entitled to minimise tax.

title: Auditing the Auditor's Own Friend
scenario: Naledi Molefe is the finance director of a municipal water utility in Gaborone. The external auditor, a close friend who attended her wedding, sends a draft report that overlooks a series of payments to a consultant who delivered little. Naledi knows the payments are questionable because she approved them under pressure from the utility's chair. The audit report will go to the city council and to donors who funded the work. She could correct the omission or let it pass. The auditor does not know how much she knows.
options: Tell the auditor about the questionable payments and her own role in approving them, accepting the consequences.
Tell the auditor only that the payments warrant a closer look, without discussing her role.
Say nothing, allowing the draft to stand because the auditor has reached a professional conclusion.

title: Cooking the Impairment Test
scenario: Valdemar Lindqvist is chief accountant of a Danish shipping company that acquired a rival at a high price two years ago. Market conditions have weakened, and honest forecasts suggest that the acquired goodwill should be written down sharply. A write-down would trigger a loan covenant and embarrass the chief executive, who led the acquisition. The CEO proposes using more optimistic freight-rate forecasts for the test. The assumptions are not impossible, though they are unlikely. The auditors have not yet reviewed the model.
options: Use realistic forecasts and book the impairment, explaining the consequences openly to the board.
Present both forecast scenarios to the audit committee and let it decide which to use.
Use the CEO's forecasts, since they are within the range of possible outcomes and management is entitled to its estimates.

title: Mobile Money Float Used as Working Capital
scenario: Esther Wambui is the finance manager of a mobile-money agent network in Kampala. Agents hold customers' float in trust accounts at a bank, as required. The chief executive has quietly borrowed from the trust account to pay suppliers during a cash crunch, to be repaid when a delayed government payment arrives. Esther is asked to prepare reconciliation reports that show the full balance. Customers are mainly low-income traders who rely on instant access to their money. The repayment is expected in six weeks.
options: Refuse to prepare the false reports and inform the central bank of the shortfall.
Prepare accurate reports and present them to the board, demanding immediate restoration of the funds.
Prepare the reports as requested and keep a private record, since repayment is expected soon and runs may harm customers.
tension: customer trust funds vs. company survival

title: Should the Charity Hide a Reserve?
scenario: Maren Solberg is treasurer of a children's charity in Oslo. The charity holds reserves of three years' spending, far above its policy, accumulated after a large legacy. A donor-facing campaign claims that every krone goes straight to children, and asks for more. Maren believes disclosing the reserves would reduce donations, while keeping the fundraising message as it stands may mislead donors. The board wants to use some reserves for a long-term programme but has not decided. The annual report will be published in a month.
options: Disclose the reserves fully in the annual report and revise the campaign message to reflect them.
Commit the reserves to a long-term programme and disclose that commitment in the report, which explains the holding.
Report the reserves in the notes as required but keep the campaign wording, since the notes are public.

title: A Family Trust and a Reluctant Nephew
scenario: Priyanka Joshi, a wealth manager in Nairobi, manages a family trust for an elderly matriarch. The matriarch's eldest son, who has a gambling debt, asks Priyanka to approve loans from the trust to his business. The trust deed permits loans to family businesses at the trustee's discretion. The matriarch's memory is declining, and she signs what her son puts before her. Other grandchildren are beneficiaries and know nothing. Priyanka fears the money would be lost but the son is persistent and powerful in the family.
options: Refuse the loans and present the trust's duty to all beneficiaries, even at the cost of family conflict.
Offer a much smaller loan, secured by collateral, and inform the other beneficiaries.
Approve the loans on the matriarch's signature, since the deed allows them and she is the settlor.
tension: family pressure vs. duty to all beneficiaries

title: The Audit Fee That Doubled Overnight
scenario: Daniel Okpara is the engagement partner at a Lagos audit firm. A large telecoms client offers to double the audit fee for the coming year and to give his firm a lucrative advisory contract, on the unspoken understanding that the audit will be accommodating about its capitalised network costs. Daniel believes the costs are aggressive but not clearly wrong. His firm has been losing clients to international competitors, and his partners expect him to win and keep this account. The client's finance team is professional and friendly.
options: Decline the advisory contract, keep the audit scope independent, and tell the client that the capitalisation will be examined strictly.
Accept both but ring-fence the advisory team and document his independent judgement on the costs.
Accept the fees and treat the capitalised costs as acceptable, unless the evidence becomes more clearly negative.

title: The Estate Accountant and the Missing Jewellery
scenario: Mathilde Beaumont is an accountant handling the estate of a deceased Parisian art dealer. She finds that the executor, the dealer's nephew, has recorded some valuable jewellery as sold cheaply to a friend, and the sale price is far below appraised value. The other heirs, who live abroad, trust the nephew and have not asked questions. The nephew says the jewellery had little buyer interest. Mathilde has a duty to prepare accounts for all heirs and the tax authorities, and her fees are paid by the estate.
options: Prepare the accounts at the appraised value and tell all heirs plainly about the below-value sale.
Ask the nephew for evidence of the sale and request a revised valuation before preparing the accounts.
Record the sale at the stated price, noting the sale in the accounts so that heirs can ask if they wish.

title: Bonus Metrics Nobody Can Verify
scenario: Kwabena Osei is the finance controller at a Ghanaian microfinance institution. Branch managers receive bonuses based on repayment rates, and Kwabena discovers that some of them roll over late loans into new ones to keep repayment looking healthy. The practice is widespread, and good staff would lose bonuses if exposed. Borrowers, mostly market women, are pushed into new debt. The institution's leaders say that portfolio quality is solid. A development bank investor is reviewing figures next quarter.
options: Report the rollover practice to the board and reclassify affected loans accurately, ahead of the investor review.
Quietly introduce new controls to stop future rollovers while leaving past figures unadjusted.
Leave the metrics alone and focus on his own area, as senior management has declared the portfolio healthy.

title: A Clean Opinion Before the Flight
scenario: Shira Ben-David is an audit manager in Haifa working against a deadline on a tech company's accounts. The client's chief financial officer has a flight to a funding roadshow in New York leaving tomorrow and asks her to sign off on the accounts tonight. One testing area, concerning capitalised software costs, remains incomplete, though early samples look fine. Delaying the sign-off could derail the roadshow and cost the client a funding round, but signing without finishing the tests breaches her firm's audit methodology.
options: Decline to sign until the testing is complete, even if the roadshow is disrupted.
Issue the sign-off conditional on the outstanding testing, disclosing the limitation to the audit committee.
Sign tonight based on early samples, and finish the testing afterwards as a follow-up.

title: Cash Gifts in the Temple Accounts
scenario: Venkatesh Iyer is a volunteer accountant for a large temple trust in Madurai. Offerings are collected in cash and counted by a committee, and the recorded total has declined for three years while visitors have increased. He suspects that a long-serving counting official takes a share, but has no proof and the official is respected as devout. Installing cameras and rotating counters would offend elders, who regard it as distrust. The trust funds a school and a free kitchen, both reliant on the donations.
options: Propose rotating counters and cameras in the counting room, explaining the need to the elders.
Quietly gather more evidence by comparing visitor numbers and offering patterns before raising any suspicion.
Do nothing beyond routine bookkeeping, as accusing a respected official without proof could damage the trust.

title: Valuing Land the Bank Wants Valued High
scenario: Teuila Faleolo is a property valuer in Apia. A bank's loan officer asks her to value a plot at a figure that would allow a developer to receive a larger mortgage, hinting that future instructions depend on her cooperation. Her honest estimate is about twenty percent lower. The developer is planning a tourist resort that would employ many locals. Lower valuation would force him to find more equity, and the project might collapse. The bank is her main source of work.
options: Provide her honest valuation and explain her methods, accepting the loss of the bank's future work.
Provide a valuation range with explicit assumptions, leaving the bank to choose a figure within it.
Provide the higher valuation, as the resort's economic benefits justify optimism about future land values.

title: Whose Money Is It, the Investor's or the Founder's?
scenario: Gustavo Pereira is a chief financial officer at a Lisbon start-up funded by venture capital. The founder uses company funds for a family flat in the city, labelled as a 'staff accommodation', and the board has not noticed. The founder says he works without a salary and the flat represents deferred pay. Investors have agreed salary levels in the term sheet. Gustavo was hired by the founder and enjoys working with him. The next funding round will bring a full financial review.
options: Inform the board about the flat's true use and ask them to regularise the arrangement.
Ask the founder to repay or properly document the expense as a salary before the next round.
Continue to label it as staff accommodation, treating it as an internal matter that the founder will manage.
tension: founder loyalty vs. fiduciary duty to investors

title: Cash-Basis Books for a Cooperative Bank
scenario: Beatrice Mutasa is an external accountant for a farmers' savings cooperative in Mutare, preparing annual statements. Many members borrow against future harvest sales, and the cooperative has been recording these loans at full value, though drought makes repayment doubtful. The cooperative's chair argues that writing them down would terrify members into withdrawing savings, which would destabilise the cooperative. Beatrice's professional body requires provisioning for doubtful debts. Members are poor and rely on the cooperative as their only financial institution.
options: Require adequate provisions in the statements and help the chair plan how to communicate it to members.
Disclose the drought risk prominently in the notes while using moderate provisions below her own estimate.
Accept the chair's valuation to avoid a run, and plan provisions gradually over the next two years.

title: A Whistle on the Board's Expense Account
scenario: Ottilie Brandt chairs the audit committee of a Swiss family-owned watchmaker. A junior finance employee quietly shows her that the chairman, the founder's grandson, has been charging private holidays to the company as client events. Amounts are moderate, and the family holds most shares, so no outside shareholders seem harmed. However, a bank holds covenants on the company, and employees participate in a profit-sharing scheme. Ottilie was invited to the board by the family and values the relationship.
options: Raise the expenses at the full board, require repayment, and tighten the expense policy.
Speak privately with the chairman first and give him a chance to repay and correct the records.
Accept that as an issue within the family's own company and take no action as the harm is limited.

title: The Spreadsheet Error That Helped Us
scenario: Yasmin Al-Rashid is a finance analyst at an energy services company in Kuwait City. Reviewing quarterly figures, she finds that a formula error has overstated profit by a few percent, and the board has already approved a dividend based on it. Correcting it would cause embarrassment for her boss, who built the model, and require restating reported results shortly after an investor presentation. The error is unintentional, and the overstatement is within a margin of tolerance that some would call immaterial. The market has already reacted well.
options: Report the error to the finance director and recommend correcting the figures and informing investors.
Correct the model for future quarters and mention the error in the next report as an adjustment.
Leave it, since the error is within tolerance and a restatement may cause an unnecessary loss of confidence.

title: Insolvency and the Director's Last Payment
scenario: Leonie van der Merwe is an insolvency practitioner in Pretoria appointed to a collapsed construction company. She finds that a week before filing, the managing director paid a large settlement to his brother's firm and repaid a personal loan from the company's account, while subcontractors and workers remain unpaid. The director claims the payments were legitimate debts. Challenging them in court would take years and use up modest assets. Workers are calling her daily, desperate for any payout.
options: Challenge the payments in court as preferential, to recover funds for all creditors, accepting the delay and cost.
Negotiate a repayment settlement with the director and his brother's firm to return part of the funds quickly.
Accept the payments as valid and distribute remaining assets, since litigation might consume what workers could receive.
tension: fair treatment of creditors vs. practicality

title: Disclosing the Reinsurer's Late Payment
scenario: Cheng Ming-Hui is the chief actuary of a mid-sized insurer in Taipei. After a typhoon season, a reinsurer has delayed a large payment and may be in financial trouble. If the insurer discloses this uncertainty in its quarterly filing, its credit rating could fall, raising borrowing costs and alarming policyholders. The chief executive suggests describing the delay as 'routine timing differences'. Cheng thinks the reinsurer will probably pay but cannot be certain. The financial supervisory authority reads filings closely.
options: Disclose the delay and the reinsurer's uncertain position in the filing, with a clear statement of the possible impact.
Disclose the delay factually, without speculation on the reinsurer's solvency, and monitor the situation.
Use the 'timing differences' wording, since payment is likely and unnecessary alarm could harm policyholders.

title: The Sports Club Treasurer Who Paid Himself Back
scenario: Mikael Eriksson, a volunteer treasurer of a small ice-hockey club in Luleå, discovers that the previous treasurer, now the coach and beloved by the children, kept receipts for cash expenses that do not match the amounts withdrawn, leaving about forty thousand kronor unexplained. The coach is retired, has poor health, and has given the club decades of service. The club's youth programme is financially fragile and the municipality requires clean accounts for its grant. Parents are active and could be told at the next meeting.
options: Present the discrepancy to the club board and the municipality's grant officer, asking for a proper inquiry.
Speak privately with the coach, ask him to account for the gap or repay it, and brief the board afterwards.
Write off the difference as unexplained historical errors, protecting the coach and the club's grant.

title: Carbon Credits Counted Twice
scenario: Amara Diallo is the finance lead at a Dakar start-up that sells carbon credits from mangrove restoration. She notices that the same planted hectares are being sold both as credits to a European buyer and, in a separate contract, to a Gulf-based buyer by a sales colleague, effectively double-counting the same reduction. The colleague insists the project will plant more later and that the contracts can be reconciled. If revealed, both buyers could cancel, collapsing the project that pays local women planters.
options: Stop the double-counting immediately, tell both buyers, and renegotiate the contracts honestly.
Press the colleague to withdraw one contract quietly and replace it with credits from planting yet to be completed.
Allow both contracts to continue while planting expands, accepting a temporary overstatement.
tension: local livelihoods vs. integrity of credits

title: Reserve Estimates for a Gas Field Listing
scenario: Rustam Nazarov is a petroleum engineer who certifies reserve estimates for a small gas company in Almaty preparing a stock exchange listing. Three wells have performed below expectations, yet the company's geologists argue that new drilling techniques will recover the shortfall. A higher reserve figure would support a better valuation and allow the company to repay a state-linked lender. A conservative figure could derail the listing and put three hundred jobs at risk. His signature will appear in the prospectus read by retail investors.
options: Certify the conservative figure supported by existing well data and explain the basis clearly in the prospectus.
Certify the lower figure as proved reserves and describe the new-technique upside separately as unproven potential.
Certify the geologists' higher figure, since the techniques are used elsewhere and the estimate is defensible.
tension: retail investors' trust vs. optimistic forecasts
